fact_en: Did you know iron nails actually get heavier when they rust? That's because the iron chemically combines with invisible oxygen from the air around it!
fact_bis: Nahibaw-an ba nimo nga ang mga pako nga puthaw mo-gain og mas bug-at kung mag-oxidize? Nagkombinar man gud ang puthaw sa dili makita nga oxygen gikan sa hangin!

findings.note: Tagalog false friend in BOTH title and body. EN 'Rust Makes Nails Heavy' / 'iron nails get heavier when they rust' becomes title_bis 'Kalawang Bug-at Pako' and body 'ang mga pako nga puthaw mo-gain og mas bug-at kung mag-oxidize'. In Cebuano pako = WING (pako = nail only in Tagalog); the Cebuano for nail is lansang. A child reads 'iron wings', and nothing in the card ever names a nail, so the object of the fact is never restored.

fact_en: An anvil is a heavy, solid metal tool! It provides a hard surface for hammering and shaping other heated metals.
fact_bis: Ang anvil kay usa ka bug-at, solidong metal nga gamit! Naghatag kini og hugot nga surface para sa pag-martilyo ug pag-hubog sa ubang init nga metal.

findings.note: Tagalog false friend: 'hubog' is Tagalog for shape/mold, but in Cebuano 'hubog' means DRUNK. title_bis 'Anvil Metal Martilyo Hubog' reads 'Anvil Metal Hammer Drunk', and the body repeats it: 'para sa pag-martilyo ug pag-hubog sa ubang init nga metal' = 'for hammering and getting the other hot metals drunk'. Nothing on the card restores 'shaping' (Ceb. hulma/porma), so the anvil's stated purpose is lost in both the headline and the body. Compounded by 'hugot nga surface' (tight) for 'hard surface' (gahi).

fact_en:
What is frost on mountain grass?

Frost is water vapor changing directly into solid ice crystals! It forms on high altitude mountain grass without becoming liquid water first.
fact_bis:
Unsa ang hamog sa sagbot sa bukid?

Ang hamog kay singaw sa tubig nga nag-direct nga nahimong solid ice crystals! Kini motubo sa sagbot sa taas nga bukid.

findings.note: The body names frost "hamog", which in Cebuano is DEW/mist — the corpus uses it that way consistently (ffct-07275 breath condensing into "klarong hamog", ffct-09610 "tulo sa hamog" on a spiderweb, ffct-15853 fog). So the Cebuano card asserts that dew is water vapour turning DIRECTLY into solid ice crystals, which is false of dew and erases the deposition-vs-condensation point the card exists to teach. The sibling card in the same batch (ffct-21067) shows the right word: "escarcha (frost)". Only the bare English token "Frost" in title_bis hints at the intended referent, and it is never defined in Cebuano.

fact_en:
How do we separate solid mixtures like flour?

We use a sieve! It's a handy tool that separates solid mixtures based on particle size.
fact_bis:
Unsaon pagbulag sa solid nga halo sama sa harina?

Naggamit tag sieve! Kini usa ka tool nga nagbulag sa solid nga halo base sa particle size.

findings.note: "Unsaon pagbulag sa solid nga halo sama sa harina?" — "halo" is Tagalog for mixture; in Cebuano halo is the MONITOR LIZARD (this corpus itself glosses it that way in ffct-00855: "Ang halo (monitor lizard)..."). Cebuano for mixture is sagol, used correctly in sibling cards (ffct-21116, ffct-21152). The card uses "halo" twice and never says sagol, so the Cebuano-only child is told a sieve separates a solid lizard by particle size.

fact_en: A native Philippine striped snakehead mudfish burrowing in wet soil creates a cool heterogeneous mixture of dirt and water!
fact_bis: Ang native Philippine striped snakehead mudfish nga nag-ukay sa basa nga yuta nagbuhat ug heterogeneous mixture sa dirt ug water!

findings.note: title_bis "Dalag ug Yuta" for "Mudfish and Soil". In Cebuano dalag = YELLOW (Tagalog false friend: dalag = mudfish in Tagalog only); this corpus uses dalag for yellow throughout (ffct-00296 "dalag nga dahon", ffct-00403, ffct-00853). Cebuano for the snakehead mudfish is haluan/aluan. The body never uses any Cebuano fish name (it keeps the English "striped snakehead mudfish"), so the headline a child sees reads "Yellow and Soil" and is never corrected.

fact_en:
What happens to fruit peels in compost?

In the decomposition stage of composting, bacteria chemically break down solid fruit peels into nutrient-rich soil matter over several weeks!
fact_bis:
Unsay mahitabo sa panit sa prutas sa compost?

Sa decomposition stage sa composting, chemically gibuungkag sa mga bakterya ang solid fruit peels into nutrient-rich soil matter sulod sa pipila ka semana!

findings.note: title_bis "Compost Balat Baktirya Yuta" for "Compost Peels Decompose". In Cebuano *balat* is the SEA CUCUMBER (trepang); peel/skin is *panit* — *balat* is the Tagalog word. The headline a child sees therefore reads "compost sea-cucumber bacteria soil", naming a different thing than fruit peels. The body does use "panit sa prutas" correctly, so this is a title-only defect, but it is the class of Tagalog false friend the sweep is hunting. Fix: "Compost Panit Baktirya Yuta".

fact_en:
Why is bamboo so lightweight but strong?

Bamboo is a highly renewable grass with hollow internodes that give it low density, making it a lightweight but strong construction material!
fact_bis:
Ngano nga gaan apan lig-on ang kawayan?

Ang kawayan kay usa ka highly renewable nga grass nga naay hollow internodes nga naghatag og low density, mao nga gaan apan lig-on kini nga construction material!

findings.note: title_bis "Kawayan Wala Tibay" for "Bamboo Hollow Strong". *Wala* is not Cebuano for hollow (that is *lungag* / *walay sulod*); read as written the three-word title parses as "walay tibay" = bamboo has NO strength — the exact reverse of the card's point, and the reversal sits in the headline. The body ("gaan apan lig-on") states the fact correctly, so the contradiction is resolvable by reading on, but the title alone asserts the opposite. Fix: "Kawayan Lungag Lig-on".

fact_en: The bark of the Philippine narra tree contains tannins with high solubility, meaning they dissolve easily in liquid water!
fact_bis: Ang kahoy sa Philippine narra tree adunay tannins nga taas ang solubility, mao nga dali ra kini matunaw sa liquid water!

findings.note: EN: "The BARK of the Philippine narra tree contains tannins...". BIS: "Ang KAHOY sa Philippine narra tree adunay tannins..." — bark in Cebuano is 'panit (sa kahoy)'; 'kahoy' is the wood/tree itself. The Cebuano relocates the tannins from the bark to the wood and nothing in the card corrects it (title is just 'Solubilidad'). Construction is also garbled ('the tree of the narra tree'), which suggests 'bark' was simply dropped rather than translated. Fact as stated in the card body is changed and unrecoverable.

fact_en: Inhaling aerosol sprays like air fresheners can irritate your lungs! This happens because liquid droplets are suspended in a gas.
fact_bis: Ang paglanghap sa aerosol spray sama sa air freshener makairita sa baga! Tungod kini kay ang likido nga patak naglutaw sa gas.

findings.note: title_bis "Aerosol sa BAGANG" — 'bagang' is a MOLAR TOOTH in Cebuano; lungs is 'baga'. The headline therefore points at the teeth on a card about lung irritation (title_en: 'Aerosols Irritate Lungs'). Caveat for ranking: the body DOES say 'makairita sa baga' correctly, so a child who reads past the headline recovers the right organ — flagged only because the title is the headline and the swap is a one-letter organ substitution that will recur; treat as title-only repair, not a body defect.

fact_en:
How can a neodymium magnet separate iron nails from copper coins?

A neodymium magnet attracts ferromagnetic materials like solid iron nails! This separates them from non-magnetic solid copper coins.
fact_bis:
Unsaon pagbulag sa neodymium magnet sa mga pako ug mga sensilyo?

Ang neodymium magnet makadani og ferromagnetic materials sama sa solid iron nails! Mabuhat niini ang pagbulag sa non-magnetic solid copper coins.

findings.note: Question line: "pagbulag sa neodymium magnet sa mga pako ug mga sensilyo" — pako in Cebuano is a WING (Tagalog pako = nail; Cebuano nail = lansang). A child reads "separate the wings from the coins", so the Cebuano question is unanswerable as written. Restoration exists only via the untranslated English "solid iron nails" in the body, not via any Cebuano word.

fact_en:
What happens when you light a Sinulog candle?

It melts the solid wax into a liquid, which then vaporizes to fuel the burning flame!
fact_bis:
Unsay mahitabo kung pasigaon ang kandila sa Sinulog?

Matunaw ang solidong wax ngadto sa liquid, unya mo-vaporize aron mapaka-poy ang nagdilaab nga kalayo!

findings.note: EN: melted wax "vaporizes to fuel the burning flame". BIS: "unya mo-vaporize aron mapaka-poy ang nagdilaab nga kalayo" — a Cebuano reader parses mapaka-poy as pakapoy (kapoy = tired/weakened), so the card says the vapour TIRES OUT / weakens the flame, the reverse of fuelling it. Nothing else in the card restores the direction; the causal fact the card exists to teach (wax vapour is what burns) is lost.

fact_en:
Is milk a true solution or something different?

Milk is a colloid, not a true solution, because its suspended fat and protein particles are large enough to scatter light! 🥛
fact_bis:
Ang gatas ba tinuod nga solusyon o lahi?

Ang gatas usa ka colloid, dili tinuod nga solusyon, kay ang suspended fat ug protein particles niini dako kaayo nga makapahimulos sa kahayag! 🥛

findings.note: EN reason: particles "are large enough to scatter light". BIS: "dako kaayo nga makapahimulos sa kahayag" — pahimulos = to benefit from / take advantage of, not to scatter (mokatag / motibulaag sa kahayag). The whole explanatory mechanism that distinguishes a colloid from a true solution is replaced by a meaningless claim and is not restored anywhere else on the card.
